faq.a: Yes. The Moon spins once on its axis about every 27.3 days, exactly the time it takes to go round Earth once. That is why it seems not to turn.

faq.q: Why does the Moon spin at exactly that speed?
faq.a: Long ago the Moon spun faster. Earth's gravity raised bulges on it, and Earth's pull on those bulges gradually slowed its spin until one turn matched one orbit. This is called tidal locking.

faq.q: Is there a dark side of the Moon?
faq.a: Not really. The far side, which we never see from Earth, gets as much sunlight as the near side. At new moon, the far side is fully lit. A better name is the far side.
asks: Is the far side of the Moon dark?

faq.q: Who first saw the far side of the Moon?
faq.a: The Soviet probe Luna 3 photographed it in 1959. The first people to see it with their own eyes were the Apollo 8 astronauts, who orbited the Moon in December 1968.
asks: What does the far side of the Moon look like?

faq.a: Yes, most large moons are, including Jupiter's big moons and Saturn's moon Titan. Pluto and its moon Charon are both locked, always showing each other the same face.
asks: Do other planets' moons show one face?

facts: The Moon rotates once every 27.3 days, the same time it takes to orbit Earth.
Because of slight wobbles called libration, about 59 percent of the Moon's surface can be seen from Earth over time.
The Soviet probe Luna 3 took the first photographs of the Moon's far side in October 1959.

quiz.why: The Moon is tidally locked: its 27.3-day spin matches its 27.3-day orbit, so one face always points at Earth.
